title: Ratios: part-to-part and part-to-whole
blurb: Write and simplify ratios in the right order, turn part-to-part ratios into fractions of the whole, and share or change amounts in a ratio.
question: In a nursing cohort of 63 students, the ratio of women to men is 7:2. The HESI A2 asks how many men there are, what fraction of the cohort is men, and how many more women than men there are. How does one ratio answer all three?

teach.body: Formally, a ratio compares two or more quantities by division and can be written a:b, a to b, or a/b. In plain English: a ratio says 'for every 7 of these, there are 2 of those'. It does not tell you the actual counts until you know one count or the total. The order of the words decides the order of the numbers: women to men 7:2 is men to women 2:7.

teach.h: Boys to girls is 3:2 in a class of 35
teach.caption: To use a part-to-part ratio on a total, add the parts first: one part = 35 ÷ 5 = 7.

teach.h: Worked example: sharing in a ratio
items: Split $500 in the ratio 2:3:5. Add the parts: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts.

teach.text: A 3:2 ratio does NOT mean 3/2 or 60% of anything by itself. With boys to girls 3:2, boys are 3/5 (60%) of the class and girls are 2/5 (40%). And order matters: 'girls to boys' is 2:3, the reverse of 3:2. HESI options are built from exactly these slips: the reversed ratio, the part-to-part fraction, and the other group's count.

teach.h: Simplify like a fraction, after matching units
teach.body: Divide both terms by their greatest common factor: 16:24 = 2:3 (divide by 8). If the terms carry units, make the units match FIRST: 2 feet to 8 inches is 24 inches to 8 inches, so 3:1, not 1:4. Clear decimals by multiplying both terms by the same number: 1.5:2 = 3:4. 'In lowest terms' means no whole number above 1 divides both terms.

teach.caption: Units first, then divide both terms by the same number.

teach.h: Worked example: one count gives you the rest
items: RNs to LPNs is 5:3, and there are 24 LPNs. LPNs are 3 parts, so one part = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 nurses.
How many more RNs than LPNs? (5 − 3) parts × 8 = 16. Check: 40 − 24 = 16. ✓
Divide by the part you KNOW (3 for LPNs), never by the other term.

teach.h: Changing a ratio: 12 RNs, 20 aides, target 4:5
teach.caption: Find the size of one part from the group that does NOT change.

items: Aaliyah's nursing cohort has 63 students; women to men is 7:2. Total parts: 7 + 2 = 9. One part: 63 ÷ 9 = 7.
Fraction that is men: 2 parts of 9 = 2/9 (about 22.2%), not 2/7.
How many more women than men: (7 − 2) × 7 = 35. Check: 49 − 14 = 35. ✓

teach.h: A 1:4:15 cleaning mix, 2,000 mL in all

items: Order matters: a:b means a first, in the order the words give.
Simplify by dividing both terms by the same number, after making units match.
Part-to-part 3:2 means part-to-whole 3/5 and 2/5: add the parts for the whole.
Known count ÷ its own ratio term = one part; multiply for every other group.
To change a ratio, size one part from the group that stays fixed.

summary: You can now write a ratio in the order asked, simplify it after matching units, and switch between part-to-part ratios and fractions or percents of the whole. You can also share a total in a two- or three-part ratio, find every count from one known count, and work out how many must be added to reach a new ratio.

A.q: In a nursing cohort of 63 students, the ratio of women to men is 7:2. How many of the students are men?
A.why: Total parts: 7 + 2 = 9. One part: 63 ÷ 9 = 7. Men: 2 × 7 = 14. Check: 49 women + 14 men = 63, and 49:14 = 7:2. ✓

whyNot.0: 18 treats the ratio as a fraction of the whole (2/7 × 63); men are 2/9 of the cohort.
whyNot.3: 9 divides 63 by 7 instead of by the 9 total parts.

A.q: Write the ratio 45 minutes to 2 hours in lowest terms.
A.why: Match units: 2 hours = 120 minutes. 45:120. Divide both terms by 15: 3:8.

whyNot.0: 8:3 reverses the order; the minutes are named first.
whyNot.1: 45:2 compares minutes with hours without converting.
whyNot.3: 9:40 uses 100 minutes per hour (45:200). An hour has 60 minutes.

A.q: In a survey of 120 clinic patients, the ratio of satisfied to unsatisfied patients was 7:3. How many patients were unsatisfied?
A.why: Total parts: 7 + 3 = 10. One part: 120 ÷ 10 = 12. Unsatisfied: 3 × 12 = 36. Check: 84 + 36 = 120. ✓

whyNot.0: 84 is the number of satisfied patients (7 parts).
whyNot.1: 40 divides 120 by 3, treating the 3 as the number of parts.
whyNot.2: 51 takes 3/7 of 120, treating the part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole.

B.q: On a unit, the ratio of LPNs to RNs is 2:5. There are 35 RNs. How many LPNs are on the unit?
B.why: RNs are 5 parts: one part = 35 ÷ 5 = 7. LPNs: 2 × 7 = 14. Check: 14:35 = 2:5 (divide by 7). ✓

whyNot.1: 87.5 scales the wrong way (35 × 5 ÷ 2), as if the RNs were the 2 parts.
whyNot.2: 49 is the total number of nurses (7 parts), not the LPNs.
whyNot.3: 21 is how many more RNs there are than LPNs (3 parts).

B.q: Write the ratio 1.2 L to 300 mL in lowest terms.
B.why: Match units: 1.2 L = 1,200 mL. 1,200:300. Divide both terms by 300: 4:1.

whyNot.0: 1:4 reverses the order; the 1.2 L is named first.
whyNot.2: 1:250 compares 1.2 with 300 without converting liters to milliliters.
whyNot.3: 40:1 converts 1.2 L to 12,000 mL. One liter is 1,000 mL.

B.q: A cleaning solution mixes bleach, detergent and water in the ratio 1:3:16. How many milliliters of detergent are in 4 L of solution?

whyNot.0: 200 mL is one part, the amount of bleach.
whyNot.1: 750 mL uses 3/16 of 4,000, comparing detergent with water instead of with the whole.

C.q: On a hospital unit the ratio of RNs to LPNs is 5:3, and there are 24 LPNs. Six more RNs are hired. What is the new ratio of RNs to LPNs, in lowest terms?
C.why: One part = 24 ÷ 3 = 8, so there are 5 × 8 = 40 RNs. After hiring: 46 RNs to 24 LPNs. 46:24 simplifies to 23:12 (divide by 2).

whyNot.1: 4:3 adds the 6 new staff to the LPNs (40:30) instead of the RNs.
whyNot.2: 11:9 adds 6 to each number in the ratio. Ratios change by recounting, not by adding to the ratio terms.
whyNot.3: 23:15 adds 6 to both counts (46:30); only the RNs increased.

C.q: On a pediatric ward, the ratio of boys to girls is 3:4. After 6 more boys are admitted and no girls, the ratio becomes 1:1. How many girls are on the ward?
C.why: Let one part = x: boys 3x, girls 4x. After admissions, 3x + 6 = 4x, so x = 6. Girls: 4 × 6 = 24. Check: boys 18 + 6 = 24, so 24:24 = 1:1. ✓

whyNot.0: 18 is the number of boys before the admissions.
whyNot.2: 6 is the size of one part, not the number of girls.
whyNot.3: 42 is the total number of children before the admissions (7 parts).

C.q: In a patient survey, the ratio of patients who rated their care 'excellent' to those who did not is 7:3. What percent of patients rated their care 'excellent'?

whyNot.0: 233.3% treats 7:3 as 7/3; a part-to-part ratio must be turned into part-to-whole first.
whyNot.2: 42.9% is 3/7, comparing the two groups with each other in reverse.
whyNot.3: 30% is the share who did NOT rate their care excellent.

reteach.title: Lemonade by the scoop
reteach.question: A lemonade recipe uses 2 scoops of powder for every 5 cups of water. How does thinking in 'batches' solve every ratio question?

blocks.body: One batch is 2 scoops + 5 cups = 7 units. Any amount of this lemonade is just some number of batches. For 840 units in total, you need 840 ÷ 7 = 120 batches, so 2 × 120 = 240 scoops and 5 × 120 = 600 cups. If you only know the powder (say 30 scoops), that is 30 ÷ 2 = 15 batches, so 15 × 5 = 75 cups of water.

blocks.text: The batch size is the SUM of the parts. Dividing the total by just one part (840 ÷ 5) mixes up part-to-part and part-to-whole.

explain.body: A ratio like 2:5 compares two parts. To find a share of a total, add the parts (2 + 5 = 7), divide the total by that sum, then multiply by the part you want.

items.label: saline as a fraction of the mix
water as a fraction of the mix

test.q: Saline and sterile water are mixed in the ratio 2:5 to make 840 mL. How much saline is in the mixture?
test.why: Total parts: 2 + 5 = 7. One part: 840 ÷ 7 = 120 mL. Saline: 2 × 120 = 240 mL. Check: 240 + 600 = 840. ✓

whyNot.0: 336 mL uses 2/5 of 840, treating the part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole.
whyNot.1: 120 mL is one part, not the 2 parts of saline.
whyNot.3: 600 mL is the sterile water (5 parts).

explain.body: Write both terms in the same unit, then divide both by their greatest common factor. 40 minutes to 1.5 hours becomes 40 minutes to 90 minutes.

test.q: Write the ratio 40 minutes to 1.5 hours in lowest terms.
test.why: 1.5 hours = 90 minutes. 40:90. Divide both terms by 10: 4:9.

whyNot.0: 9:4 reverses the order; the 40 minutes are named first.
whyNot.1: 80:3 doubles 40:1.5 without converting hours to minutes.
whyNot.3: 2:5 uses 100 minutes for 1 hour (40:100). An hour has 60 minutes.

explain.body: Add all the parts to get the batch size. One part = total ÷ batch size. Then multiply by the part you need.

test.q: A fruit punch mixes orange, pineapple and cranberry juice in the ratio 4:3:1. How much pineapple juice is in 6 L of punch?
test.why: Total parts: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. One part: 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 L. Pineapple: 3 × 0.75 = 2.25 L. Check: 3 + 2.25 + 0.75 = 6. ✓

whyNot.0: 3 L is the orange juice (4 parts).
whyNot.2: 0.75 L is one part, the cranberry juice.
whyNot.3: 4.5 L takes 3/4 of 6, comparing pineapple with orange instead of with the whole punch.

explain.body: Keep the group that does not change. Use it to find one part of the NEW ratio, then compare with the current count.

test.q: A clinic has 18 male and 24 female volunteers. How many more male volunteers are needed so that the ratio of males to females is 5:6?
test.why: Females stay at 24 = 6 parts, so one part = 4. Males needed: 5 × 4 = 20. Add 20 − 18 = 2. Check: 20:24 = 5:6. ✓

whyNot.0: 6 is the number needed for a 1:1 ratio (24 − 18), not 5:6.
whyNot.1: 20 is the total number of males needed, not how many more.
whyNot.3: 5 is the males' ratio term, not a count of volunteers.
